title: Breaking the Chain of Teacher Burnout (And How I Fixed My Planning Process)
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele describes the 'Chain of Burnout,' in which unsupported lesson planning traps teachers in a cycle that too often ends in attrition. When a department has no bank of high-quality, ready-to-go lessons, teachers design slides almost from scratch, which eats the time they would otherwise spend rehearsing explanations and behaviour management; tired teaching produces woolly explanations and classroom struggle, which produces negative observation feedback, which culminates in the belief 'I'm not a good teacher' and exit from the profession. While acknowledging systemic fixes (union conversations about workload, building a centralised lesson bank), Emanuele shares a practical four-step 'Silver Bullet' workflow for producing quality quickly: batch-process every 'Do Now' starter first to break the psychological barrier, use a custom Gemini planner that applies atomisation while the teacher acts as editor, generate activities and matching worksheets with an HTML creator, and package the deck and worksheets with an answer key.
points: The root problem is a department with no bank of ready-to-go lessons, leaving teachers to build decks from scratch or rebuild disorganised materials — often at 2:00 AM for an 8:30 AM lesson.

The 'Chain of Burnout' runs from excessive planning time, to no time to rehearse, to woolly explanations and weak behaviour management, to negative observations, to 'I'm not a good teacher,' to leaving.
Systemic remedies matter — talking to unions about workload and pushing departments to build a centralised, consistent lesson bank — but individual workflow fixes can help right now.

The four-step 'Silver Bullet' workflow: batch all 'Do Now' starters first, use a Gemini planner that atomises while the teacher edits, generate activities and worksheets via an HTML creator, then package with an answer key.
The AI keeps the teacher 'in the driver's seat' by removing blank-page paralysis rather than replacing professional judgement.
quotes: You find yourself exactly where I was 11 years ago (and, let’s be honest, where I still find myself occasionally): sitting in the glow of a laptop screen at 2:00 AM, desperately trying to plan a lesson for 8:30 AM the next day.

Too many colleagues, Senior Leadership Teams, and university mentors treat the too long lesson planning as “just part of the job.” But it isn’t just an inconvenience. It is the start of a dangerous chain reaction.
You convince yourself, “I’m not a good teacher,” and you give up.
You must push your department to build a centralised, consistent lesson bank, stopping the 'freedom to teach' from turning into anarchy.
This keeps the teacher in the driver’s seat but removes the “blank page” paralysis.
As I often say, there is no single “silver bullet” in teaching. But my goal is to give you a toolbox full of silver bullets so you can choose the right one for the monster you’re fighting that day.
